short_title: Cumulative LDL-C exposure in young adulthood and middle age (4 pooled US cohorts)

citation.title: Association Between Cumulative Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Exposure During Young Adulthood and Middle Age and Risk of Cardiovascular Events

access.full_text_source: PubMed Central article page (PMC8459309), converted to text; figure images not inspected

study.design_detail: Pooled data from ARIC, CARDIA, Framingham Offspring and MESA. LDL-C trajectories from age 18 were modelled with multiple imputation (30 imputed data sets); cumulative LDL-C (area under the trajectory, mg/dL × years), time-weighted average (TWA) LDL-C and LDL-C slope were computed up to the index visit (last visit aged 40-60 with measured LDL-C). Cox models with age as time scale, stratified by cohort; quartile comparisons and splines.
study.population: Participants of 4 US cohorts with 2 or more LDL-C measures at least 2 years apart between ages 18 and 60, at least one at ages 40-60, without CVD before the index visit; mean age 56.4 years at index visit, 56.4% women, 71.0% non-Hispanic White
study.exposure_or_intervention: Cumulative LDL-C, TWA LDL-C and LDL-C slope from age 18 to the index visit (partly imputed)
study.comparator: Top vs bottom quartile of each LDL-C variable; models with and without adjustment for LDL-C at the index visit
outcomes: Incident coronary heart disease (myocardial infarction or CHD death)
study.follow_up: Median 16 years after the index visit

source_location.quote: A total of 18 288 participants were included in this study.
During a median follow-up of 16 years, 1165 CHD, 599 ischemic stroke, and 1145 HF events occurred.

findings_summary: In 18 288 adults from four US cohorts followed for a median of 16 years, higher cumulative and time-weighted average LDL-C from age 18 to midlife were associated with higher incident coronary heart disease. Comparing top with bottom quartiles, the hazard ratio for cumulative LDL-C was 1.97 when adjusted for standard risk factors and 1.57 when further adjusted for the single LDL-C measured in midlife; for time-weighted average LDL-C the corresponding values were 1.95 and 1.69. LDL-C slope was not associated with CHD after adjusting for midlife LDL-C (0.88). None of the LDL-C variables was associated with ischemic stroke or heart failure.

limitations.text: Early-life LDL-C was largely not observed: trajectories from age 18 were estimated by multiple imputation, so cumulative exposure is partly modelled rather than measured.

The authors argue imputation error was likely nondifferential and biased toward sample means, making the estimates conservative (toward the null). This argument does not address bias from the pooled trajectory model itself.
Possibly underpowered for ischemic stroke and for racial and ethnic minority subgroups.
Observational associations: they do not show that lowering LDL-C earlier changes outcomes, although they are consistent with other evidence the authors cite.
Hazard ratios are relative comparisons of extreme quartiles; the paper's text reports no absolute CHD risks by quartile.
Supplementary material (eFigures, eTables including event counts by quartile) and figure images were not reviewed for this record.

applicability_constraints: US cohort participants with at least two LDL-C measurements between ages 18 and 60, one at ages 40-60, and no CVD before the index visit.
Cumulative exposure is defined from age 18 to the index visit; the quartile cutoffs describe this pooled sample only.
Group-level hazard ratios over a median 16 years; not an individual's risk.

discrepancies.description: The Abstract reports the adjusted CHD hazard ratios (1.57, 1.69, 0.88) without stating that they compare top with bottom quartiles; the Results text states the comparison.
discrepancies.handling: Record labels them as top vs bottom quartile, per the Results text.

discrepancies.description: The exposure window is described as 'from age 18 to 60 years' in the Abstract but as from age 18 to the index visit (last visit aged 40-60) in the Methods.
locations: Methods, 'Cumulative LDL-C, TWA LDL-C, and LDL-C Slope'
discrepancies.handling: Record uses the Methods definition (age 18 to the index visit).

interpretation: The study supports the idea that a single midlife LDL-C does not capture everything about past LDL-C exposure that is associated with coronary disease: long-term averages remained associated after adjusting for the midlife value. It also shows the main practical obstacle. Even large cohorts rarely measured LDL-C across young adulthood, so the exposure was partly imputed from models. For one person, historical laboratory records can document LDL-C at the dates it was actually measured. They cannot establish exposure during unmeasured years without assumptions, and those assumptions should be explicit rather than hidden in a single 'cumulative' number.
